statement: Ten counters lie in a row: five black ones followed by five white ones. A move swaps a black counter with the white counter directly to its right. Moves are made, in any order, until no move is possible. How many moves are made in total?

choices.misconception: I counted the 9 gaps between neighbouring counters and allowed one swap for each gap.
I thought each of the ten counters moves exactly once.
I counted every pair of counters, $\binom{10}{2} = 45$, but only pairs with a black counter to the left of a white one ever swap.
I counted each swap twice, once for the black counter and once for the white one.

hints: Look at pairs made of one black and one white counter.
Find a quantity that every move changes by exactly one, such as the number of pairs with a black counter somewhere to the left of a white one. It fixes the number of moves in any order.
At the start all $5 \times 5$ black and white pairs have the black counter on the left. Each move fixes exactly one such pair, and the process stops only when none are left.

solutions.reliable: Call a pair made of one black and one white counter out of order if the black one is to the left of the white one. At the start all $5 \times 5 = 25$ such pairs are out of order. A move swaps two neighbours, so it changes the order of exactly that one pair and no other: the count drops by exactly 1. If any pair is out of order, somewhere a black counter has a white counter directly to its right, so a move is still possible; the process therefore stops exactly when the count reaches 0. So exactly 25 moves are made, whatever their order. The transferable idea: a quantity that changes by exactly one per move counts the moves for you.
solutions.elegant: Each white counter must end up to the left of every black counter, and in one move it passes exactly one black counter. Each of the 5 white counters passes 5 black ones, so there are $5 \times 5 = 25$ moves. The transferable idea: count how many times each object must overtake another.

whyOnTest: A process with free choices still has a fixed length when some quantity drops by exactly one each move, which turns a search into a count.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
